message.content: {"outcome":"DIRECT_SUB_OPTIMAL","best_model_id":"PGS003972","confidence":"Moderate","rationale":"All 6 candidates are direct matches (trait_reported/efo and phenotyping_reported are abdominal aortic aneurysm; one is explicitly prevalent AAA but still aligned). Among them, PGS003972 (Nat Genet 2023 AAA GWAS meta-analysis; PRS-CS; very large multi-cohort development list including ARIC/HUNT/MVP/UKB/deCODE/eMERGE) is the most disease-focused multi-cohort option, which domain guidance prefers over pan-trait/portability framework scores when endpoint alignment is similar. Competing candidates include (i) PGS001784 (Cell Genom ‘Global Biobank’ framework) and (ii) PGS002054 (AJHG ‘Portability of 245 polygenic scores’ UKB framework), both of which are framework/portability-derived despite large validation and some PRS-only/partial-r metrics; (iii) PGS003429 is from a screening cost-effectiveness framing with unknown covariates and only full-model AUROC reported; (iv) PGS000753 is older, very sparse (29 SNP) and prevalent endpoint. Limitation: PGS003972’s reported discrimination is only a full-model AUROC (0.69) without an explicit PRS-only metric, and PGS003973 reports a much higher full-model C-index (0.882) but could be largely covariate-driven and is not directly comparable; this incomplete/heterogeneous metric reporting prevents a high-confidence ‘best’ choice."}

The most disease-focused, endpoint-specific option with clean/basic covariates and an explicit PRS effect size is PGS000753 (MVP/Mayo AAA paper; OR per SD=1.37 [1.30–1.44] in European validation), which provides direct evidence of PRS contribution without relying on potentially covariate-driven full-model AUROC. Limitation: the newer AAA-focused PRS-CS models (PGS003972/PGS003973) are also disease-focused, but only full-model AUROC/C-index is visible and covariates are unknown/partially specified, so the available evidence does not cleanly establish which is superior on PRS-only performance; thus the recommendation remains sub-optimal rather than high-confidence."}
